title: What Lovable is and what problem of yours it solves
promise: You'll know how to decide, with your specific case in front of you, whether Lovable works for you or is going to waste an afternoon, and you'll have your account set up and your first screen in the browser without writing a single line of code.
why: Carmen runs an accounting firm with four employees. She's spent a year and a half asking for quotes on a website where her clients could upload their quarterly invoices instead of sending them over text at eleven at night. The cheapest quote was $3,600 and four months. She let it drop. One Saturday morning she wrote what she wanted into Lovable, in plain English and one paragraph, and forty minutes later she had a page with her logo, an upload form, and a list of what had come in. It wasn't finished and it wasn't perfect: it didn't tell one client from another and anyone with the link could get in. But for the first time she had something to show and decide about, instead of a quote to think over.

theory.title: You talk to it in plain English and it hands you back a working website
theory.text: Lovable is a webpage where you write what you want to build, in your own language and words, and it builds the application in front of you: the screens, the buttons, the forms, and the database where what people type gets stored. It doesn't give you instructions to do it yourself; it does it and shows it to you working in the right half of the screen. You look, say what's wrong, and it changes it.
theory.analogy: The difference from asking a chat for code is the same as the difference between someone explaining over the phone how to assemble furniture, and someone coming over, assembling it in your living room, and asking if you want it further to the left.

theory.title: What you're really buying is the first version
theory.text: The value isn't that it builds you the final application, because it won't. It's that in one afternoon you go from an idea in your head to something you can open, show, and criticize. That changes every conversation that follows: with your partner, with your client, with a developer you hire. Discussing a screen that exists is infinitely faster than discussing a document describing it.
theory.example: Carmen showed her screen to two clients. In ten minutes they told her something that was in no quote: that they wanted to see the history of previous quarters. In the $3,600 version, that would have been a mid-project change order.

theory.title: Where it wins and where it loses
theory.text: It wins at anything that's screens, forms, lists, dashboards, and pages: a company website, a form that saves data, an internal dashboard for your team, a small tool your people use daily. It loses once you get into complex business rules, odd integrations with old programs, high concurrent traffic, or serious legal requirements. It's not that it can't; it's that at that point you need someone who can read what it's written.
theory.analogy: It's a lightning-fast cook for a twenty-dish menu. For a wedding banquet with allergies and intolerances, you still need a head chef.

visual.title: Does your idea fit what Lovable does well?
visual.caption: Answer with your case in front of you. It's the question that saves you an afternoon.
visual.question: What's the main thing your application needs to do?

branches.why: Exactly its territory: a company website, a form that saves data, an internal dashboard, a small tool for your team. You'll have something working this afternoon.

branches.answer: Business rules with lots of exceptions
branches.then: It's going to struggle, and so will you
branches.why: If your invoices carry a surcharge that only applies to out-of-state customers in the last quarter, it won't guess that. It can be done, but at that point you need someone who can read what it's written.

branches.answer: Connecting to an old company program
branches.then: Depends on whether that program has an API
branches.why: If it does, it's doable. If it's a fifteen-year-old desktop program with no way to talk to it from outside, no tool fixes that: that's a separate project.

branches.answer: Lots of people using it at once, or sensitive data
branches.then: Start here, but plan for help
branches.why: For showing and deciding, it's perfect. Before real people with real data go in, accounts, permissions, and a security review need to happen, and it's worth having someone check that.

theory.title: The code is yours, and that matters more than it looks
theory.text: Everything it builds stays in a GitHub project you can download. This isn't a technical detail: it's your insurance. It means that if Lovable raises prices, shuts down, or you stop liking it one day, your work isn't held hostage inside its website. Any developer can take that code and keep going. It's the difference between renting and holding the deed.
theory.example: Connect your project to GitHub on day one, even if you don't know what GitHub is. It's a button. You'll understand it in lesson 16 of the path; what you don't want is to remember this six months from now.

visual.title: What you keep and what stays behind if you ever leave
visual.caption: Click each piece. It's what decides whether your work is held hostage or not.

nodes.label: The code
nodes.does: Everything it builds stays in a GitHub project you can download. It's standard code: any developer can pick it up and continue.
nodes.input: Connected with one button, on day one.
nodes.output: A repository with your files and their history.
nodes.breaks: If you don't connect GitHub, your work lives only inside this website.

nodes.label: The database
nodes.does: The data people type into your forms lives in a separate service, under your account. It isn't inside Lovable.
nodes.input: Connected when you set up user accounts.
nodes.output: A database of your own, with its tables.
nodes.breaks: Until you connect it, you're running on whatever Lovable sets up by default.

nodes.label: The chat and the versions
nodes.does: The conversation, the change history, and the way of editing by talking: that lives here and nobody takes it with them.
nodes.breaks: If you leave, you lose this. You still have the code, but you go back to editing it by writing it.

nodes.label: The hosting
nodes.does: The address where your application is published while you use Lovable.
nodes.breaks: The address changes if you leave, unless you have your own domain. Set that up before handing out the link.

theory.title: The real limit isn't the tool, it's what you ask it
theory.text: The number one reason people give up isn't that Lovable fails. It's that they ask for "a management app" and get something generic and watered-down, or they ask for twenty things at once and everything comes out half-baked. This tool responds to detail: who logs in, what they see, what they can do, what happens when they make a mistake. The more specific you are, the better it comes out, and that specificity is yours to provide, not its.
theory.analogy: It's like ordering a suit. "A blue one" and "navy blue, slim fit, two buttons, no pleats, and unhemmed trousers" end up as two very different suits.

theory.title: Credits: what you spend is per message, not per minute
theory.text: Lovable doesn't charge by time, it charges per instruction you send it. The free plan gives a handful of messages a day, enough to test and build a first screen, and it runs out faster than you'd think if you correct one thing at a time. The habit that saves the most credits is writing one well-thought-out message instead of five short ones correcting yourself.
theory.example: Five messages saying "make the button bigger," "now blue," "now centered," "a bit lower," "okay, smaller" use up five times more than one single message describing how you want the button.

visual.title: One well-written message versus five short ones
visual.caption: Same final result, very different spend. Watch the credits at each step.

steps.label: Five short messages
steps.why: Five credits for one change. And each rebuild can break something that already worked, so sometimes it's five credits and a new problem.

steps.label: One thought-out message
steps.does: The whole change described at once, numbered
steps.why: One credit. Plus, writing it all out forces you to decide what you actually want, which improves the result before you even send it.

steps.label: The long initial request
steps.does: Who logs in, what they see, what they do, what you don't want
steps.why: The most cost-effective of all. Whatever you don't explain, it'll assume, and then it costs ten messages to straighten out.

tasks.title: Write what you want to build, before opening anything
tasks.where: On paper, in a notes app, or wherever you write
tasks.action: In five lines and without using a single technical word: who's going to log into this, what they see when they arrive, what they can do, what happens when they do it, and how you'll know it worked. Write it even if it seems obvious. This paper is what you'll paste later, and it's what separates a useful result from a generic one.
tasks.expect: A paragraph someone else could read and understand what this is without you explaining it to them.
tasks.stuck: If nothing comes out, just answer this: what is someone doing by hand today that you want them to stop doing? That sentence is your project.

tasks.title: Create the account
tasks.action: Go in and click the sign-up button. Signing in with your Google account is the fastest and saves you making up another password. No card needed to start: the free plan is available from minute one.
tasks.expect: You land on a screen with a big text box in the center asking what you want to build.
tasks.stuck: If the confirmation email doesn't arrive in five minutes, check spam. Watch for lookalike domains: the real address is lovable.dev, nothing in front of it.

tasks.title: Check how many credits you have before spending them
tasks.where: In your avatar, top right, inside Settings
tasks.action: Find the plan or credits section and write down two numbers on your paper: how many free messages you get a day and when they reset. Data as of August 2026. Check it yourself, since these plans change every few months.
tasks.expect: You know exactly how many attempts you have today. That changes how you write your first message.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find the counter, send any message: once sent, the usage often shows up somewhere on screen.

tasks.title: Send your first request, the long one
tasks.where: In the big box in the center
tasks.action: Paste the prompt below with your details inside. It's deliberately long: every line you cut is a decision it's going to make for you.
tasks.prompt:
I want to build a simple web application. I'll describe the whole thing before you start, and I want you to build it all at once, not in pieces.

WHAT IT IS: [ONE SENTENCE. EXAMPLE: a site where my clients upload their quarterly invoices]

WHO LOGS IN: [WHO. EXAMPLE: my accounting clients, ages 40 to 65, half from mobile]

WHAT THEY SEE WHEN THEY ARRIVE: [THE FIRST SCREEN. EXAMPLE: a page with my logo, a welcome line, and a big upload button]

WHAT THEY CAN DO, in order of importance:
1. [THE MAIN THING. EXAMPLE: upload one or more PDF files or photos]
2. [THE SECOND THING. EXAMPLE: type their name and the quarter these correspond to]
3. [THE THIRD THING. EXAMPLE: see the list of what they've already uploaded, with the date]

WHAT HAPPENS AFTER: [EXAMPLE: they see a "received" message and I can review everything uploaded from a separate screen]

HOW I WANT IT TO LOOK: clean, lots of white space, large legible type, and works well on mobile. Colors: [TWO COLORS, OR SAY "the ones from my logo" AND UPLOAD THE LOGO]. No animations or gradients.

IN ENGLISH: all on-screen text in plain English, including error messages and buttons.

TWO THINGS I DON'T WANT YET: don't set up user registration or passwords, and don't connect payments. We'll cover that later.

Before building anything, tell me in five lines what you've understood needs to happen and what you had to assume because I didn't tell you. Wait for my confirmation.
tasks.expect: It answers with a summary of what it understood and a list of assumptions. Read it: that's where you'll see what you hadn't explained well.
tasks.stuck: If it starts building without asking you, let it finish and then write: "stop, tell me what you assumed that I didn't tell you."

tasks.title: Read the assumptions and correct before it builds
tasks.where: In the chat on the left
tasks.action: From the list of assumptions it gave you, pick the wrong ones and reply with only those, numbered. Don't use this to ask for new things: that comes later. Here you only correct what it misunderstood.
tasks.expect: It confirms the changes and starts building. Screens start appearing on the right.
tasks.stuck: If all the assumptions look fine to you, just say "correct, go ahead."

tasks.title: Open it and use it as if you were your customer
tasks.where: In the preview, the right half of the screen
tasks.action: Don't look at whether it's pretty. Do what the person it's for would do: fill out the form, upload a file, click the button. Then break it on purpose: hit submit without filling anything in, type a hundred-character name, upload a huge file.
tasks.expect: A written list of what didn't work. Almost certainly nothing happens, or something odd happens, when you submit empty: that's normal for a first version.
tasks.stuck: If the preview is blank or errors out, go to step 8: it's the most common thing on day one.

tasks.title: Test it on an actual phone
tasks.action: Find the share button or public preview link and open it on your phone. Half the users of anything you build will come in from there, and screens that look perfect on a computer often break on a narrow screen.
tasks.expect: You know whether buttons are tappable with a finger and whether you have to zoom to read anything. Write it down.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find the public link, on the computer you can narrow the browser window down to phone width: it'll do to get by.

tasks.title: Correct everything at once, not five times
tasks.action: Take the list from steps 6 and 7 and write one single message with everything that needs fixing, numbered. Every separate correction costs you a credit, so bundling them isn't just tidier: it's cheaper.
tasks.prompt:
I've tested the application and found these things. Fix all of them in this same change, not one at a time:

1. [WHAT HAPPENS] · It should [WHAT SHOULD HAPPEN INSTEAD]
2. [WHAT HAPPENS] · It should [WHAT SHOULD HAPPEN INSTEAD]
3. [WHAT HAPPENS] · It should [WHAT SHOULD HAPPEN INSTEAD]

Also, check these three things I know tend to be missing and fix them if they are:
- That submitting the form empty shows a clear warning in English saying which field is missing, instead of doing nothing.
- That while something's being sent, it's visible that it's happening, so nobody clicks the button three times.
- That on mobile you don't have to zoom to read or to tap the buttons.

When you're done, tell me in two lines what you changed.
tasks.expect: It rebuilds and the bugs on your list disappear. Check it yourself, don't just trust it saying it's done.
tasks.stuck: If fixing one thing breaks another, point out both: "fixing X broke Y, I want both working."

tasks.title: Connect it to GitHub today, not six months from now
tasks.where: In the project menu, looking for GitHub
tasks.action: Click connect and follow the steps. If you don't have a GitHub account, create one: it's free and takes two minutes. You don't need to understand what it is yet. All you're doing is making your work exist outside this website too.
tasks.expect: A new repository appears in your GitHub account with your project's name and files inside.
tasks.stuck: If it asks for permissions and that makes you uneasy, grant them only for that repository, not your whole account: GitHub's screen lets you choose.

tasks.title: Decide, in writing, whether this continues or stays here
tasks.where: On the same paper from step 1
tasks.action: Write three lines: what you achieved in this session, what's the first thing missing for someone to actually use it, and whether, based on what you've seen, it's worth continuing. It's a legitimate decision to say no. What's not legitimate is not deciding and coming back in three weeks remembering nothing.
tasks.expect: A written answer to "do I continue?" If yes, you now know the next piece.
tasks.stuck: If you're unsure, the tiebreaker question is: would you show this to the person it's for tomorrow? If the answer is yes, continue.

errors.message: The preview stays blank or spinning
errors.means: What it built has a bug that stops the page from rendering. It's the most normal thing in the world on day one, and you haven't broken anything.
errors.fix: Don't fix it yourself and don't start looking at code. Write in the chat: "the preview is blank, tell me what error it's giving and fix it." It sees the error even if you don't. If after two tries it's still the same, tell it to revert the last change.

errors.means: It wrote something the computer can't read, almost always from trying to do several things at once in the same change.
errors.fix: Paste the whole error message into the chat, don't summarize it, and add: "fix this and don't touch anything else." Next time, ask for things in smaller changes: giant requests are the ones that fail most.

errors.message: Out of credits / You've reached your daily limit
errors.means: You've used up the day's messages. Nothing you've built has been lost.
errors.fix: Wait for the reset (usually every 24 hours) or move to a paid plan. Use the pause to write down everything you want to fix on paper, and tomorrow send it in one message instead of ten.

errors.message: The text comes out in another language even though you wrote in English
errors.means: By default it generates the interface in a default language; talking to it in English isn't enough on its own.
errors.fix: Tell it explicitly and all at once: "all visible text in plain English, including buttons, alerts, error messages, and help text." If new text shows up in another language later, repeat it, pointing at the screen.

errors.message: Fixing one thing broke something else that worked
errors.means: It touched more than it needed to. Happens especially with appearance changes that end up affecting logic.
errors.fix: Tell it both things together: "changing X broke Y; I want X as I asked and also Y as it was." If it gets tangled, find the project's version history and go back to the previous one.

errors.message: Anyone with the link can get in and see the data
errors.means: This isn't a bug: it's what you asked for. Until you set up user accounts, your application is open to anyone with the address.
errors.fix: Don't put a single real customer's data in there until you've set up username-and-password access. To test, use made-up names. Accounts are covered in the course's Supabase section.

errors.message: I've lost the project / I can't find yesterday's work
errors.means: Almost always you're logged out or in a different account, it's not that it got deleted.
errors.fix: Check which email you signed in with. And if you already connected GitHub in task 9, your work is there too, so it doesn't depend on this.

matters: Writing out the whole request before sending the first message. It's the difference between an application that resembles what you wanted and a generic one that later takes ten messages to straighten out. The paper from step 1 isn't paperwork: it's half the work.

Testing by breaking, not admiring. Submitting the form empty, typing where you shouldn't, and uploading a huge file teaches you more in two minutes than half an hour checking whether the colors match. The bugs you find there are exactly the ones your customer would find.

Connecting GitHub on day one. It's a button that takes thirty seconds and it's the only thing that guarantees that whatever happens with this tool or your account, your work keeps existing and someone else can continue it.

Not putting real people's data in until you have accounts and permissions. As long as the application is open by link, anyone who has it can get in. A customer's name and phone number in there is a real problem, not a test.
ignore: Colors, fonts, and overall look during the first session. Changing that is fast and happens at the end; fighting with it at the start burns credits you need for the application to do what it's supposed to do.

The code that shows up if you click the code tab. You don't need to understand it to work this way, and looking at it now only stresses you out. Its moment will come, and it'll be when you want to change something very specific.

Custom domains, payments, multiple languages, and anything that sounds like "and also." Each of those is a whole lesson later on. Cramming them into the first afternoon is the surest way to finish nothing.
canDo: Build you, in one afternoon, something that opens in the browser, can be shown, and can be critiqued: screens, forms, lists, dashboards, and pages that save what people type.

Translate your plain-English description into reasonable technical decisions without asking you anything: which database, which structure, how the screens are organized. To start out, those decisions are usually good.
Correct things on what already exists. You point out what's wrong in plain language, pointing at the screen, and it changes it without you having to explain where that is in the code.
Leave your project in GitHub, in a standard format any developer can pick up and continue. It doesn't lock you into this tool forever.
cantDo: Understand your business. If your invoices carry a surcharge that only applies to out-of-state customers in the last quarter, it won't guess that: you have to explain it, in those words.
Guarantee that what it built is secure. It can leave a screen open to anyone with the link and not warn you, because you never asked it not to. Security has to be explicitly requested and checked.

Sustain a large application with years behind it. As it grows, changes start breaking distant things, and that's when you need someone who can read what's written. That moment arrives, and it's not a failure: it's success.
Work well with vague requests. "Make me a management app" produces something generic that's useless. The specificity has to come from the person, and that's the part that can't be delegated.
words: Prompt
What you write to it. It's the request, in plain everyday language. Here it's deliberately long, not a loose sentence.
Preview
The right half of the screen, where you see your application actually working while it builds it. It's not a picture: you can click it.
Credit
What you spend every time you send it an instruction. The free plan gives a few a day and they run out faster if you correct things one at a time.
Repository
Your project's folder with its entire history. It's what gets created on GitHub when you connect it, and it's your real backup.
Deploy
Taking your application out of preview and putting it on an internet address other people can visit.
Database
The filing cabinet where what people type into your forms gets stored. Lovable sets it up on its own, without asking.
Authentication
The username-and-password system. Until you set it up, your application is open to anyone with the link.
Responsive
That the screen adapts to phone width without needing to zoom. Checked on an actual phone, not by imagining it.
Build
The moment it turns what it's written into a website you can open. If it fails, you get "build failed" and nothing shows.
Version
A saved state of your project. Used to go back when a change made everything worse.

pieces.title: Before showing it to anyone
pieces.caption: Seven checks. The first three are the ones that prevent a real problem.
items: There's not a single real customer's data inside: only made-up names
You know whether anyone with the link can get in and see the data
GitHub is connected and the repository has files inside
You've opened it on an actual phone, not just imagined it
You've submitted the form empty and get a clear warning, not silence
The text is in English, including error messages
You've written down what it's missing for someone to actually use it
